specPoints.text: evaluate data to explain the necessity, for many industrial processes, to reach a compromise between the yield and the rate of reaction

primer.text: Industry cannot maximise yield, rate and cost at once, so it negotiates. Using the Haber process as the arena, this note prices the temperature and pressure compromises - 450 degrees, 20 megapascals, roughly a third conversion - and weighs finance, energy and safety against every extra percent.

lessons.title: The Haber compromise: yield against rate and cost
lessons.opening: The Haber process squeezes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen, and every condition chosen is a treaty between thermodynamics and economics: 450 degrees for speed-with-yield, 20 megapascals for acceptable cost, and a catalyst to make it all brisk.
keyPoints: Haber equilibrium: N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, exothermic in the forward direction.
Higher temperature raises rate but lowers yield, since the equilibrium shifts left; higher pressure raises yield (4 reactant moles versus 2 product moles).
About 450 oC and 20 MPa (200 atmospheres) give roughly 35 percent yield in acceptable time; doubling pressure to 40 MPa adds only about 7 percent.
The compromise weighs financial cost, energy and environmental needs, and worker safety against yield.

low.restatement: Cold gives yield but no speed, hot gives speed but no yield, huge pressure gives yield but costs a fortune - so industry plants the flag at 450 oC and 20 MPa and recycles unreacted gas instead.
low.analogy: Farming a slow crop in a short season: you plant at the date that balances ripeness against the calendar, not the date that maximises either alone.
low.examPointer: Quote both conditions with their numbers (450 oC, 20 MPa, ~35 percent) and name all three compromise considerations for evaluation questions.

medium.restatement: The 4-to-2 gas mole imbalance makes pressure the thermodynamic ally and the accountant's enemy; temperature is the pure trade - kinetic gains against equilibrium losses - so the chosen 450 oC is a productivity optimum, not a thermodynamic one.
medium.analogy: A bicycle gear: neither the hardest nor the easiest gear maximises distance per hour; the middle gear does.
medium.examPointer: Connect each condition to its Le Chatelier effect AND its cost effect - one without the other is half an answer.

check.stem: Increasing the temperature of the Haber process raises rate but lowers yield because

options.text: The forward reaction is exothermic, so heating shifts the equilibrium leftward
options.explanation: Extra heat drives the endothermic backward direction, cutting ammonia while speeding collisions.

options.text: The forward reaction is endothermic, so heating favours products
options.explanation: The forward Haber reaction releases heat; it is exothermic.

options.text: High temperature destroys the catalyst
options.explanation: The iron catalyst survives at 450 oC.

options.text: Hydrogen decomposes at high temperature
options.explanation: No such decomposition drives the yield loss.

check.stem: Increasing pressure raises ammonia yield because

options.text: Four gas moles of reactants become only two moles of product, so the position shifts right
options.explanation: The fewer-mole product side relieves the pressure rise.

options.text: Two moles become four, so the position shifts right
options.explanation: The mole ratio runs 4 reactants to 2 products.

options.text: Pressure raises the temperature of the gases
options.explanation: Pressure shifts equilibrium; heating shifts it left.

options.text: The catalyst works better under pressure
options.explanation: Catalysts change rate, not position.

check.stem: Industry uses about 450 oC rather than a lower temperature because

options.text: Lower temperatures give too slow a rate despite higher equilibrium yield
options.explanation: Yield without speed is unproductive; 450 oC balances the two.

options.text: Lower temperatures cost more energy
options.explanation: Heating less costs less; the reason is rate.

options.text: 450 oC maximises the equilibrium yield
options.explanation: Lower temperatures would give higher yield.

options.text: The catalyst only functions at 450 oC
options.explanation: Catalysts function across a temperature range.

check.stem: Doubling the Haber pressure to 40 MPa adds only about 7 percent yield, so industry keeps 20 MPa because

options.text: The extra yield does not repay the financial, energy and safety costs of higher pressure
options.explanation: Diminishing returns versus multiplying costs kills the upgrade.

options.text: Higher pressure lowers the yield
options.explanation: Higher pressure raises yield here, just modestly.

options.text: 40 MPa is below the catalyst's tolerance
options.explanation: The constraint is economic, not catalytic.

options.text: Pressure cannot be varied once set
options.explanation: Plants routinely engineer pressure ranges.

check.stem: Which considerations balance the Haber compromise?

options.text: Financial and profit, energy and environmental, health and safety
options.explanation: All three consideration families shape the final conditions.

options.text: Colour of ammonia, smell of hydrogen, taste of nitrogen
options.explanation: None of these is a real consideration.

options.text: Only the equilibrium constant
options.explanation: The compromise is economic as much as thermodynamic.

options.text: Only the speed of the catalyst
options.explanation: Rate is one factor among several.

check.stem: State the temperature and pressure used in the Haber process.
State the approximate ammonia yield at the compromised conditions.
check.modelAnswer: Roughly 35 percent of the reactants convert to ammonia per pass.

check.stem: Explain why the Haber process needs a compromise of conditions at all.
check.modelAnswer: The conditions that maximise yield (low temperature, high pressure) slow the rate or raise costs intolerably, so temperature and pressure are chosen to balance yield, rate, expense and safety.

check.stem: A proposal suggests running Haber at 550 oC to triple the rate. Evaluate with Le Chatelier reasoning.
check.modelAnswer: Rate would rise but yield would fall, since heating shifts the exothermic equilibrium left; combined with higher energy cost, the proposal likely fails the yield-time-economics test that 450 oC currently wins.

glossary.definition: The fraction of reactants converted into the desired product per pass through the process.
Reaction conditions chosen to balance yield, rate, cost and safety rather than maximise any one.
The share of reactant stock turned into ammonia per pass, roughly 35 percent at the compromised conditions.

workedExample.prompt: The exam hint frames the temperature compromise as: is it better to produce 100 g of ammonia per hour or 1000 g per day? Decide with arithmetic.
steps: Convert the hourly option to a daily figure: 100 g per hour times 24 hours.
Compare 2400 g per day against 1000 g per day, noting the hourly plant also delivers product continuously.
workedExample.finalAnswer: 100 g per hour wins: 2400 g per day beats 1000 g per day, so accepting a slower rate but steady production is the better compromise.
